doc.title: Curtis Fuller — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Avant-garde ideas of Russell, Dave Baker and Oliver Nelson
summary: Fuller and Brower discuss how Baker's and Russell's theory stayed rooted in tradition.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: But, you're so grounded in the literature and in the various languages that you are supposed to be able to mentally do this. If your orientation is about the ear, than that’s another piece.

That’s another part about that. From that I graduated to… What's his name? It was jazz and poetry. He would come through with a tuxedo and sneakers. Playing (scats abrasive solo) I'll be playing so nicely, and JJ and all the trumpet players would come and say, "See what he does with this!” After I heard Dave Baker and adapted to him…
So, this was after Dave had that accident and he wasn't…
Okay, So he was still playing bone. So, he and George Russell were kind of taking this theoretical thing.

Oh, they were taking that. They took it. They did it. It made sense because they were coming from style. If you go back and listen to “Down by the Riverside” and stuff like that, there is a lot of style there. You can still hear some Fletcher Henderson, even though it was avant garde. You could still hear that. Eldon also followed suit. Like everybody else like me, I thought it was, you know…
As things came from Oliver Nelson, we were moving, we were flowing we were creating things. If you’re an artist, you don’t want to be left out.
